clue.text: Assumed spies engaged in airlift at sea

indicators.note: the spies are engaged in, held within, the scrambled letters of the airlift
at sea means confused or all over the place, so the letters of airlift are rearranged

parts.note: the CIA is the American spy agency

explanation.surface: A false identity used by spies caught up in an airlift operation over the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assumed' looks like a verb about spies taking cover identities; it is the adjective meaning fake. 'at sea' scrambles the airlift and 'engaged in' holds the spies.
explanation.definitionFit: Something assumed, like an assumed name, is put on rather than real, hence false or man-made.

clue.text: A girl has bottom pinched, unfortunately

indicators.note: the girl's bottom, her last letter, is pinched, stolen away

parts.note: lass is a common word for a girl

explanation.surface: A young woman has her behind groped, which is regrettable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pinched' plays on the cheeky surface: the girl's last letter is stolen, as 'has bottom pinched' says.
explanation.definitionFit: Alas is an exclamation of regret, used where one might say unfortunately or sadly.

clue.text: Classified operations on Crete, possibly after onset of terrorism

indicators.note: after places the operations and Crete following the opening letter
in a down clue, on means placed above the next piece
the onset of a word is its very first letter

parts.note: OPS is the usual short form of operations, as in military ops

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters of Crete may be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Secret military operations on the island of Crete, launched after a terror attack.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'on' means above, so the operations sit over the rearranged island ('possibly'), and 'after' sets both behind the opening letter of terrorism.
explanation.definitionFit: Classified documents are restricted to authorised people, which is exactly what the most secret grade means.

clue.text: Snaps the toffee into pieces for Boxing Day

indicators.note: breaking the toffee into pieces shows its letters are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone snaps a slab of toffee into bits to share on 26 December.
explanation.walkthrough: Boxing Day, 26 December, is the British public holiday after Christmas; it is also St Stephen's Day, the feast day of the first Christian martyr.
explanation.definitionFit: Boxing Day falls on 26 December, the church's feast day honouring Saint Stephen, so the two name one date.

clue.text: Smart Conservative heading off for plant

parts.note: chic means smart and stylish

indicators.note: the head, the first letter, of the word is taken off

parts.note: a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A stylish Tory politician leaves to go to a factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' reads as a factory but means a growing plant; 'heading off' drops the first letter of the Tory.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicory is a blue-flowered plant grown for its leaves and for its root, roasted as a coffee substitute.

clue.text: Sailor, with no one else present, produces seafood

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a standard abbreviation for a sailor
to be with nobody else present is to be alone

explanation.surface: A sailor on his own serves up a fish dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Abalone is an edible sea snail, a shellfish prized as food, especially in East Asian cooking.

clue.text: Attempt from bunker, initially with wood

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of the word bunker

parts.note: ash is a tree and its timber, a type of wood

explanation.surface: A golfer tries to play out of a sand trap using a wooden club.
explanation.walkthrough: The golf picture of a bunker shot with a wood misleads; ASH is the timber.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a bash at something is informal for having a go or making an attempt.

clue.text: A fraction to one side

parts.note: a part is a fraction or portion of a whole

explanation.surface: A small portion is set aside.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing apart means being separated off, set aside from the rest, to one side.

clue.text: But not the sort of music you'd associate with steel or brass bands?

definitions.text: But not the sort of music you'd associate with steel or brass bands?

parts.words: But not the sort of music you'd associate with steel or brass bands?
parts.note: steel and brass are weighty metals, so their bands might seem to play a loud rock genre named after such material, yet steel bands and brass bands play something quite different

explanation.surface: A musing that steel bands and brass bands do not play loud rock.
explanation.walkthrough: Steel bands (Caribbean drums) and brass bands are both made of metal, yet neither plays the loud rock genre named after heavy metal.
explanation.definitionFit: The loud, distorted guitar rock genre takes its name from dense metals, the sort steel and brass are.

clue.text: Reach the headland and stop rambling

definitions.meaning: to arrive at a headland is to get to the point of land jutting into the sea
to stop wandering off the subject is to get to the essential matter

explanation.surface: A walker reaches the cape and stops wandering about.
explanation.walkthrough: A point is a headland, so arriving there literally is the first sense; 'rambling' looks like walking but means talking off the subject.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to speak directly about the key matter, while a point is also a promontory one can walk to.

clue.text: A Greek starter

definitions.meaning: the Greek letter that corresponds to A

explanation.surface: A man from Greece serves the first course.
explanation.definitionFit: Alpha is the first letter of the Greek alphabet, so it is both Greek A and the beginning.

clue.text: Lover in Italian city turned over at end of siesta

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: turned over means flipped so the city's name runs backwards

parts.note: Roma is the Italian name for Rome
taken as written

indicators.note: end of picks the last letter of siesta

explanation.surface: A lover in Rome rolls over after an afternoon nap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned over' reverses ROMA into AMOR; A is the last letter of 'siesta'.
explanation.definitionFit: Inamorata is the Italian-derived word for a female lover or sweetheart.

clue.text: Content sot, very drunk, deliberately ignored by everyone

indicators.note: a drunk person is unsteady, so the letters stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: A happy boozer, thoroughly drunk, is shunned by all the other drinkers.
explanation.walkthrough: To send someone to Coventry is a British idiom for refusing to speak to them; Coventry is a city in the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom means ostracising someone, with everyone pointedly refusing to speak to them.

clue.text: People generally in support of different afterlife

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits underneath the piece it holds up

parts.note: other means different or alternative
the world can mean people in general, as in all the world knows

explanation.surface: People in general backing a different idea of life after death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in support of' puts WORLD below OTHER in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The other world is a phrase for the realm of the dead, the life beyond this one.

clue.text: Careful in plant close to machinery

parts.note: thrift, or sea pink, is a coastal flowering plant

indicators.note: the close of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: Someone is cautious inside a factory near the machines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' reads as a factory near machinery, but it is the flower THRIFT; Y is the last letter of 'machinery'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being thrifty means spending carefully and economically, so careful with money.

clue.text: Arousing intense feeling in English grounds

parts.note: grounds for an action are its reasons, its motive

explanation.surface: Something stirs strong passions on an English sports field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grounds' suggests playing fields; here it means reasons.
explanation.definitionFit: An emotive issue is one that stirs strong emotions in people.

clue.text: Lacking information during the night?

definitions.meaning: literally in darkness, at night-time, hence the question mark

explanation.surface: Someone is unaware of what is happening after nightfall.
explanation.definitionFit: Being kept in ignorance is idiomatically being without light, so the phrase serves for both senses.

clue.text: Cars in residential areas

definitions.meaning: estate cars are British station wagons

explanation.surface: Vehicles parked around the housing developments.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain an estate is a station wagon, and also a housing development.
explanation.definitionFit: British usage calls station wagons estates and planned housing areas estates as well.

clue.text: Frodo's pony showing pace on runs

parts.note: a stride is a single pace or step
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A hobbit's little horse sets its pace on the gallops.
explanation.walkthrough: Strider is best known as Aragorn's nickname, but in The Lord of the Rings Frodo's pony on the homeward journey also bears that name.
explanation.definitionFit: In Tolkien's tale the pony Frodo rides home after the quest is named after the ranger's nickname.

clue.text: Adept, old lady's secured role

indicators.note: secured means held fast, so the mother's name holds the role inside it

parts.note: mama is a word for mother, informally the old lady; the possessive reads as has
a hat is a role, as in wearing another hat

explanation.surface: A skilled performer's elderly mother landed a part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adept' looks like an adjective but is a noun: one highly skilled or spiritually advanced. 'secured' has the old lady holding the role.
explanation.definitionFit: In Indian and Theosophical usage a mahatma is a great soul, an adept of spiritual wisdom.

clue.text: In short skirt, mother's bottom

parts.note: a miniskirt is commonly called a mini
mum is the British word for mother

explanation.surface: Mum's backside in a miniskirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottom' suggests a rear end; it means the lowest level.
explanation.definitionFit: The minimum is the lowest possible amount or level, the bottom of the range.

clue.text: Head after those who flogged cheeky kid

indicators.note: after places the head following the floggers

parts.note: people who flog others with a whip are whippers
napper is old British slang for the head

explanation.surface: A head teacher pursues the floggers of an impudent child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' looks like a headmaster chasing floggers; it is old British slang for the head, set 'after' the floggers.
explanation.definitionFit: A whippersnapper is a presumptuous, impertinent young person.

clue.text: Bury's season without foremost of wingers

indicators.note: without means lacking, so a letter is removed

parts.note: winter is one of the four seasons

indicators.note: the foremost letter of a word is its first

explanation.surface: Bury, the Lancashire football club, has a season with no wide players.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury is a town and football club in north-west England, which makes it look like a proper noun; the definition is the verb. 'without' drops W, the first letter of 'wingers'.
explanation.definitionFit: To inter is to bury a body in a grave.

clue.text: Get to know, briefly, a humorist

indicators.note: briefly means shortened, so the last letter is cut off

parts.note: to learn something is to get to know it

explanation.surface: Become acquainted for a short time with a comedian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' drops the final N of LEARN. Edward Lear was the Victorian writer of nonsense verse and limericks.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Lear was a famous writer of comic nonsense poems and limericks, so a humorist.

clue.text: Flipping angry, chasing cad in port

indicators.note: chasing means following behind, so this piece comes after the cad

parts.note: a rotter is a cad, a dishonourable man

indicators.note: flipping means turning over, so the word for angry runs backwards

parts.note: mad means angry

explanation.surface: Someone furiously angry pursues a scoundrel through the harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British swear word but is the reversal signal, and 'chasing' sets the turned word behind the cad.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotterdam is a major Dutch city and one of the busiest seaports in Europe.

clue.text: Furious, marauder at sea losing power

indicators.note: losing means a letter is dropped

parts.note: a pirate is a robber who raids ships at sea
P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: A raider on the ocean is enraged at being beaten by a stronger force.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' removes P from PIRATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Irate means very angry, furious.

clue.text: A fish out of water gulping oxygen

indicators.note: gulping means taking in, so the oxygen goes inside

parts.note: something out of the water is dry
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A fish stranded on land gasps for air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gulping' puts O inside DRY.
explanation.definitionFit: The dory, or John Dory, is a flat-bodied edible sea fish.

clue.text: Writer's book, hit, one adding fuel to the fire

parts.note: to ram is to strike with force

parts.words: one adding fuel to the fire
parts.note: a stoker tends a fire or furnace, feeding it fuel

explanation.surface: An author's novel was a hit, fanning the flames of controversy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one adding fuel to the fire' suggests a troublemaker, but it is a stoker of furnaces. Bram Stoker was the Irish author of Dracula.
explanation.definitionFit: Bram Stoker was the Irish novelist best known for writing Dracula.
